items.stem: State what is meant by the term "splash page".
items.answer: A full-page single panel used for dramatic effect
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a full-page single panel used for dramatic effect. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between a gutter and a panel.
items.answer: A panel is a framed image; the gutter is the space between panels in which the reader infers action.
items.markingKey: A panel is a framed image; the gutter is the space between panels in which the reader infers action. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why the gutter is important in graphic narratives.
items.answer: Readers must infer what happens between panels, so the gutter creates participation, ellipsis and sometimes shock. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Readers must infer what happens between panels, so the gutter creates participation, ellipsis and sometimes shock. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the following page from a graphic memoir, described in words.

[Panel 1 – wide, full width: a crowded airport arrivals hall drawn in muted greys; a small girl clutches her mother's coat. Caption: 'Toronto, 1994. Everything was too loud.']
[Panel 2 – small and square: close-up of the girl's wide eyes. No words.]
[Panel 3 – tall and narrow: an immigration officer leans over the counter; his speech balloon is filled with jagged, unreadable scribbles.]
[Panel 4: the mother's hand squeezes the girl's – the only panel in colour, a warm orange.]

Evaluate how the graphic form conveys what words alone could not.
items.answer: Panel size controls pace and emphasis: the wide establishing panel shows overwhelming space, the small square close-up isolates fear, the tall panel makes the officer loom; the unreadable speech balloon visualises the language barrier from the child's perspective; the gutters create silence between moments; colour appears only in the final panel to highlight comfort.
items.markingKey: Panel size controls pace and emphasis: the wide establishing panel shows overwhelming space, the small square close-up isolates fear, the tall panel makes the officer loom; the unreadable speech balloon visualises the language barrier from the child's perspective; the gutters create silence between moments; colour appears only in the final panel to highlight comfort. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Zara writes: "Graphic novels are easier to read than prose novels." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: They require visual literacy: readers decode panels, gutters, colour and the interplay of word and image.
items.markingKey: They require visual literacy: readers decode panels, gutters, colour and the interplay of word and image. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following two panels from a graphic novel about memory and displacement, described in words.

[Panel 1: a grandfather in a modern apartment tells a story to his granddaughter; clean lines and flat colours.]
[Panel 2: the same scene, but the apartment walls dissolve into sketchy pencil lines of a 1950s village street; the gutter between the panels has been removed, so the two images bleed into each other.]
Caption: 'He always said the village was still there, if you knew how to look.'

Analyse how the visual elements of the text contribute to its meaning.
items.answer: Clean modern lines contrast with pencil sketches; the dissolving walls visualise memory reclaiming space.
items.markingKey: Clean modern lines contrast with pencil sketches; the dissolving walls visualise memory reclaiming space. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "The graphic form can represent experience more powerfully than prose."
items.answer: Each form has distinctive powers; the graphic form excels at perception and juxtaposition.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: images create immediacy; form can show perception directly. Arguments against: prose offers interiority and nuance; images can simplify. Supported judgement: Each form has distinctive powers; the graphic form excels at perception and juxtaposition.

items.stem: Describe in words a one-page graphic sequence (four to six panels) showing a moment of tension, and explain your choices of panel size, gutter and word–image relationship.
items.answer: Indicative content: clear sequence; deliberate panel choices; commentary on pace and closure.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: clear sequence; deliberate panel choices; commentary on pace and closure.

items.stem: Explain why panel size can control pace in a graphic novel.
items.answer: Large panels slow the reader and emphasise moments; small, repeated panels speed up action or create rhythm.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Large panels slow the reader and emphasise moments; small, repeated panels speed up action or create rhythm. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the following two panels from a graphic novel about memory and displacement, described in words.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from oral testimony recorded for a museum archive (an original passage written for study).

We left at night. I don't remember much – my mother's hand, the smell of diesel, someone singing very quietly. People ask me what I felt. I was six; I felt cold. The feelings came later, much later, when I had children of my own and saw them asleep.

Analyse how the extract constructs the writer's self.
items.answer: The testimony is fragmentary – sensory details rather than narrative – and shows that trauma may be understood only later; the speaker resists the audience's expectation of dramatic emotion.
items.markingKey: The testimony is fragmentary – sensory details rather than narrative – and shows that trauma may be understood only later; the speaker resists the audience's expectation of dramatic emotion. items.stem:
Read the following extract from a memoir (an original extract written for study).

I remember the kitchen as yellow. My sister insists it was green, and she has the photographs to prove it. But I have kept it yellow for forty years, because yellow is the colour of the morning my father taught me to make bread, and I am not ready to give that morning back.

Comment on the writer's choice of language in "I remember the kitchen as yellow. My sister insists it was green".
items.answer: Contrast: "I remember the kitchen as yellow. My sister insists it was green" – the conflict between memory and evidence foregrounds the reliability of memoir.
items.markingKey: Contrast: "I remember the kitchen as yellow. My sister insists it was green" – the conflict between memory and evidence foregrounds the reliability of memoir. Read the following description of Dorothea Lange's photograph 'Migrant Mother' (1936) with its original caption.

[A black-and-white photograph. A woman in worn clothes sits under a tent, her hand raised to her chin, her eyes looking past the camera with a worried expression. Two children lean on her shoulders, faces turned away; a baby lies in her lap. The frame is tight, cutting out the surroundings.]
Caption (US Farm Security Administration file): 'Destitute pea pickers in California. Mother of seven children. Age thirty-two. Nipomo, California.'

Guiding question: How does the photograph and its caption represent poverty?
Write an analytical paragraph that answers the guiding question.
items.answer: Thesis: the image turns one woman into a symbol of a national crisis. (1) Tight framing and composition. (2) Averted gaze. (3) The caption's anonymity. Evaluation: powerful advocacy, but it raises ethical questions about consent and the subject's lack of voice.

items.markingKey: Many works convey trauma through silence, ellipsis and understatement, which can be more truthful and ethical. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following page from a graphic memoir, described in words.

[Panel 1 – wide, full width: a crowded airport arrivals hall drawn in muted greys; a small girl clutches her mother's coat. Caption: 'Toronto, 1994. Everything was too loud.']
[Panel 2 – small and square: close-up of the girl's wide eyes. No words.]
[Panel 3 – tall and narrow: an immigration officer leans over the counter; his speech balloon is filled with jagged, unreadable scribbles.]
[Panel 4: the mother's hand squeezes the girl's – the only panel in colour, a warm orange.]

Explain how composition, colour or framing are used in this text and their effect.
items.answer: Muted greys convey alienation; the officer's height in a tall panel suggests power; the warm orange in the final panel creates relief.
items.markingKey: Muted greys convey alienation; the officer's height in a tall panel suggests power; the warm orange in the final panel creates relief. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a memoir (an original extract written for study).

I remember the kitchen as yellow. My sister insists it was green, and she has the photographs to prove it. But I have kept it yellow for forty years, because yellow is the colour of the morning my father taught me to make bread, and I am not ready to give that morning back.

Explain what the extract suggests about the reliability of memory.
items.answer: The memoirist admits that her memory is factually wrong but emotionally true, showing that memoir constructs the self through selective, emotionally shaped memory rather than objective record.
items.markingKey: The memoirist admits that her memory is factually wrong but emotionally true, showing that memoir constructs the self through selective, emotionally shaped memory rather than objective record. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a memoir (an original extract written for study).

I remember the kitchen as yellow. My sister insists it was green, and she has the photographs to prove it. But I have kept it yellow for forty years, because yellow is the colour of the morning my father taught me to make bread, and I am not ready to give that morning back.

Guiding question: How does the writer explore the relationship between memory and truth?
Write an analytical paragraph that answers the guiding question.
items.answer: Thesis: the memoir values emotional truth over fact. (1) Contrasting memories. (2) Photographs as evidence. (3) The metaphor of keeping the morning. Evaluation: honesty about unreliability increases the reader's trust.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "The graphic form can represent experience more powerfully than prose."
items.answer: Each form has distinctive powers; the graphic form excels at perception and juxtaposition.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: images create immediacy; form can show perception directly. Arguments against: prose offers interiority and nuance; images can simplify. Supported judgement: Each form has distinctive powers; the graphic form excels at perception and juxtaposition.

items.stem: "Memoirists have a duty to tell the factual truth." Discuss.
items.answer: Memoirists owe honesty about what they know and do not know, even if perfect factual truth is impossible.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: readers trust the autobiographical pact; misrepresentation can harm others. Arguments against: memory is inherently selective; emotional truth matters. items.stem: "Some events are too traumatic to be represented in art." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Representation is possible and necessary, but demands ethical awareness of form and audience.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: art may trivialise suffering; aestheticising atrocity raises ethical problems. Arguments against: representation preserves memory and testimony; works like Maus show it can be done responsibly.
